ADP.title: learner transliteration
ADP.why: Until the script is learned every word is shown with its romanization, in one scheme: ch for ח and כ, ts for צ, sh for שׁ, ei for ֵי, an apostrophe before an ע / א that opens a syllable inside a word, a hyphen after a prefix (be-, le-).

ADP.title: written onto the next word
ADP.why: בְּ, לְ, מִ are prefixes, written onto the next word and fused with the article (בַּבַּיִת); the others are words of their own.

ADP.title: everyday spelling (no vowel points)
ADP.why: Everyday texts are unvocalized: the learner must read and type the standard full spelling (ktiv male), which often adds ו or י to the stripped form (שֻׁלְחָן → שולחן).

ADP.title: forms with personal endings
ADP.why: Prepositions take endings instead of pronouns, often with another stem (עִם → אִתִּי, מִ → מִמֶּנִּי, אֶת → אוֹתִי).

CCONJ.title: learner transliteration
CCONJ.why: Until the script is learned every word is shown with its romanization, in one scheme: ch for ח and כ, ts for צ, sh for שׁ, ei for ֵי, an apostrophe before an ע / א that opens a syllable inside a word, a hyphen after a prefix (be-, le-).

CCONJ.title: written onto the next word
CCONJ.why: וְ is a prefix with several spellings (וּ, וַ); אוֹ and אֲבָל are words of their own.

CCONJ.title: everyday spelling (no vowel points)
CCONJ.why: Everyday texts are unvocalized: the learner must read and type the standard full spelling (ktiv male), which often adds ו or י to the stripped form (שֻׁלְחָן → שולחן).

INTJ.title: learner transliteration
INTJ.why: Until the script is learned every word is shown with its romanization, in one scheme: ch for ח and כ, ts for צ, sh for שׁ, ei for ֵי, an apostrophe before an ע / א that opens a syllable inside a word, a hyphen after a prefix (be-, le-).

INTJ.title: everyday spelling (no vowel points)
INTJ.why: Everyday texts are unvocalized: the learner must read and type the standard full spelling (ktiv male), which often adds ו or י to the stripped form (שֻׁלְחָן → שולחן).

INTJ.title: said to
INTJ.why: Many phrases change with the person spoken to (מַה שְּׁלוֹמְךָ to a man, מַה שְּׁלוֹמֵךְ to a woman).

INTJ.title: usual reply
INTJ.why: Greetings and formulas have set answers (בֹּקֶר טוֹב → בֹּקֶר אוֹר, תּוֹדָה → בְּבַקָּשָׁה).

NOUN.title: gender
NOUN.why: Every agreeing word (adjective, verb, demonstrative, number) depends on it, and the ending often misleads (לַיְלָה m., עִיר f.).

NOUN.title: learner transliteration
NOUN.why: Until the script is learned every word is shown with its romanization, in one scheme: ch for ח and כ, ts for צ, sh for שׁ, ei for ֵי, an apostrophe before an ע / א that opens a syllable inside a word, a hyphen after a prefix (be-, le-).

NOUN.title: everyday spelling (no vowel points)
NOUN.why: Everyday texts are unvocalized: the learner must read and type the standard full spelling (ktiv male), which often adds ו or י to the stripped form (שֻׁלְחָן → שולחן).

NOUN.title: root
NOUN.why: The root letters, separated by spaces (כ ת ב): the root links the word to its family and to Arabic cognates. Loans, compounds and primary words say none, with the reason.

NOUN.title: noun pattern (mishkal)
NOUN.why: The pattern, written with the dummy root ק־ט־ל, carries meaning (places מִקְטָל, tools, professions קַטָּל) and predicts the plural and the construct. Loans, compounds and primary or one-syllable nouns say none.

NOUN.title: plural
NOUN.why: The plural is not predictable from the gender (חַלּוֹנוֹת m., שָׁנִים f.) and the stem often changes; a meaning may have its own plural (כִּכָּרוֹת squares, כִּכְּרוֹת loaves).

NOUN.title: dual (“two …”)
NOUN.why: A few nouns (units of time, paired things) say “two” with the ending ־ַיִם (יוֹמַיִם); all others use שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural.

NOUN.title: construct forms (“the … of”)
NOUN.why: Needed for every “X of Y” phrase and every compound; the stem often changes (בַּיִת → בֵּית, ־ָה → ־ַת, ־ִים → ־ֵי). The forms are also paradigm cells.

NOUN.title: forms of one meaning
NOUN.why: A meaning may use only some forms (only the plural, only the construct, only with the article, only the imperative): each such form names its meanings.

PRON.title: learner transliteration
PRON.why: Until the script is learned every word is shown with its romanization, in one scheme: ch for ח and כ, ts for צ, sh for שׁ, ei for ֵי, an apostrophe before an ע / א that opens a syllable inside a word, a hyphen after a prefix (be-, le-).

PRON.title: everyday spelling (no vowel points)
PRON.why: Everyday texts are unvocalized: the learner must read and type the standard full spelling (ktiv male), which often adds ו or י to the stripped form (שֻׁלְחָן → שולחן).

PRON.title: gender (for agreement)
PRON.why: “You” and “they” have masculine and feminine words; the verb and the adjective agree with them. both = one form for both genders; inflected = the forms carry the gender (זֶה / זֹאת).

PRON.title: forms of one meaning
PRON.why: A meaning may use only some forms (only the plural, only the construct, only with the article, only the imperative): each such form names its meanings.

VERB.title: learner transliteration
VERB.why: Until the script is learned every word is shown with its romanization, in one scheme: ch for ח and כ, ts for צ, sh for שׁ, ei for ֵי, an apostrophe before an ע / א that opens a syllable inside a word, a hyphen after a prefix (be-, le-).

VERB.title: everyday spelling (no vowel points)
VERB.why: Everyday texts are unvocalized: the learner must read and type the standard full spelling (ktiv male), which often adds ו or י to the stripped form (שֻׁלְחָן → שולחן).

VERB.title: root
VERB.why: The root letters, separated by spaces (כ ת ב): the root links the word to its family and to Arabic cognates. Loans, compounds and primary words say none, with the reason.

VERB.title: verb pattern (binyan)
VERB.why: One of paal, nifal, piel, pual, hifil, hufal, hitpael: it fixes all the forms and often the meaning relative to other verbs of the root.

VERB.title: weak-root class (gizra)
VERB.why: Explains the “irregular” forms: שׁוֹתָה, לִשְׁתּוֹת (lamed-he), בָּא (ayin-vav), תִּסַּע (pe-nun), לָלֶכֶת (הָלַךְ, irregular).

VERB.title: future (he will …)
VERB.why: The 3rd person masculine singular future is a principal part: it shows the stem vowel of pa‘al (יִכְתֹּב / יִלְמַד) and what a weak root does (יֵלֵךְ, יִסַּע).

VERB.title: preposition or object marker of each meaning
VERB.why: Each verb takes its own preposition or אֶת (definite object), often unlike English or Greek: חִכָּה לְ, עָזַב אֶת, נָהַג בְּ; none = no complement or a bare complement.

VERB.title: verbal noun (shem pe‘ula)
VERB.why: The action noun (אֲכִילָה “eating”, נְסִיעָה “a ride”) is predictable by binyan but irregular in detail, and used constantly in writing.

VERB.title: forms of one meaning
VERB.why: A meaning may use only some forms (only the plural, only the construct, only with the article, only the imperative): each such form names its meanings.
